query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor aluminum addition (e.g., approximately 2 at%) to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will promote the in situ formation of a thin, adherent Al2O3 scale during high-temperature exposure that improves oxygen resistance while maintaining the alloy's desired mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled minor addition of aluminum into the alloy (e.g., 2 at% Al) during casting to modify the oxide-forming behavior.
generation.conditions: Test in air at temperatures between 800 °C and 1000 °C for exposure times up to 5 hours; mechanical performance assessed at room temperature and at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, protective Al2O3 scale on the surface of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum, having a strong tendency to oxidize, preferentially forms Al2O3 upon exposure to oxygen. This stable, slow-growing oxide acts as a diffusion barrier, limiting further oxygen ingress and thereby preventing pesting or rapid degradation of the alloy's surface while preserving the intrinsic solid-solution microstructure that governs mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aluminum-modified alloy will demonstrate significantly reduced oxygen uptake and slower oxide scale growth compared to the untreated state, with preservation of the baseline mechanical properties (room-temperature ductility of 8–16% and high-temperature yield strength of 163–530 MPa).
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr, which, while mechanically acceptable, suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance in air at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect of the aluminum addition is anticipated to hold for exposures in air at 800–1000 °C for durations up to 5 hours; outside these conditions or with significantly different Al levels, the balance between oxidation resistance and mechanical integrity may not be maintained.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain whether a 2 at% Al addition is optimal; small changes in Al content might affect phase stability or mechanical properties, and the long-term adherence and stability of the Al2O3 scale under cyclic conditions remain to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast samples: one set of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and one set with an additional 2 at% Al. Expose all samples to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, perform microstructural and phase analysis (using scanning electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction) to assess oxide scale formation. Conduct mechanical tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C to measure tensile ductility and yield strength.
measurements: Phase composition of the surface oxide (confirmation of Al2O3 formation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-added samples do not show a significantly reduced oxide scale thickness or mass gain (indicating improved oxygen resistance) compared to the untreated samples, or if the mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) deteriorate significantly relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

decision.trend: Earlier work on refractory HEAs has often tackled high‐temperature limitations by modifying alloy chemistry or processing to trigger in‐situ secondary phase formation (for example, turning on minor oxide or intermetallic formation via Cr addition) or by controlling microstructure through thermal, mechanical, or powder‐metallurgy routes. In a related Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy, a compositional tweak was used to prevent pesting at 800 °C, and other studies have shown that processing conditions (e.g., HIP, mechanical alloying/SPS) can induce phases that influence surface reactivity and oxidation behavior. However, these interventions typically affect the bulk chemistry or phases and may compromise the inherently good mechanical properties if not carefully controlled.
decision.unsolved: For equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr the challenge remains to improve oxygen resistance during high‐temperature exposure (around 800–1000 °C for hours) without altering its beneficial ductility and strength. No prior study has specifically addressed surface oxidation protection for this exact composition via a method that isolates the surface from bulk changes.
decision.lever: Apply a thin, adherent ceramic coating (e.g., via atomic layer deposition of a self-healing alumina or similar protective oxide) to create an external diffusion barrier against oxygen ingress
decision.why: Building on the earlier results where minor compositional modifications induced beneficial in situ oxide phases for oxidation protection, a surface engineering approach offers a single, targeted intervention that shields the alloy from oxygen while leaving the bulk chemical state—and thus the room- and high-temperature mechanical performance—unchanged. A controlled oxidation test (e.g., 5-hour exposure in air at 800 °C under relevant strain rates) with the coating in place, versus an untreated control, would validate or falsify this hypothesis.
